Thirteen European hockey leagues each have a home under sportsdataverse.hockey. Unlike the HockeyTech leagues, they do not share a feed: each home wraps its league's own data source, so the function sets differ from league to league.

DEL is del_. Its docs pages use the prefix del, and its functions are del_schedule, del_pbp and so on, but the package is hockey.del_: del is a Python keyword, so import sportsdataverse.hockey.del would not parse.

Most homes have a schedule, standings, play-by-play and box scores; several add shot locations, shifts, rosters and player pages. A sample: Each home also exports its parsers (parse_liiga_games, parse_esports_pbp, ...) for working from raw payloads. The league pages list every function with its parameters and Returns table: DEL, Liiga, SHL, SIHF and the rest under Hockey in the sidebar.

Seasons are END years. season=2026 is 2025-26 in every home; each runtime maps it to its provider's own key at the boundary. Polite pacing. Every runtime leaves at least one second between one answer and the next request to the same host, retries included. Tidy by default. Wrappers return a polars DataFrame; return_parsed=False gives the raw payload and return_as_pandas=True gives pandas. from sportsdataverse.hockey.del_ import del_schedule from sportsdataverse.hockey.liiga import liiga_standings liiga = liiga_standings(season=2026) # 2025-26 games = del_schedule(season=2026) print(liiga.height, games.height) The SHL and its siblings sometimes key a call on a provider id rather than a season (shl_standings(ssgt_uuid=...)); the league page shows where that id comes from.

The PWHL and nineteen North American minor and junior leagues publish their stats through HockeyTech (LeagueStat): one query-dispatched endpoint behind every league site. sdv-py wraps it as one shared core, sportsdataverse.hockeytech, and one generated family of functions per league.

pwhl, ahl, ohl, whl, qmjhl, echl, sphl, chl, ushl, bchl, ajhl, sjhl, ojhl, cchl, gojhl, mhl, nojhl, vijhl, kijhl and mjhl, each named by its HockeyTech client code (the QMJHL's is lhjmq). Each league is a module under sportsdataverse.hockey.<league>. The PWHL lives at the top level, sportsdataverse.pwhl, with a richer surface: props, xG, ratings and release loaders. Every function is also exported from the top-level sportsdataverse namespace.

The league registry is the whole surface: each league gets the same thirteen functions, named after it. For the ECHL: The other nineteen leagues have the same thirteen with their own prefix (ohl_schedule, ushl_pbp, ...). season is the END year of the season, so season=2026 is 2025-26; the family maps it to HockeyTech's season id. Ids are Int64. import polars as pl import sportsdataverse as sdv from sportsdataverse.hockey.ushl import ushl_standings schedule = sdv.echl_schedule(season=2026) # 2025-26, one row per game standings = ushl_standings(season=2025) game_id = int(schedule["game_id"][0]) pbp = sdv.echl_pbp(game_id) print(schedule.height, standings.height, pbp.height)

The HockeyTech payloads are the same shape in every league (the seasons and scorebar rows are byte-identical across all twenty), so one parser module drives every family. The per-league differences are data, not code: the API key (public, shipped in each league's site; override with SDV_<LEAGUE>_API_KEY), the client code, and the league id the standings query takes. Some leagues publish less: ushl and mjhl play-by-play has goals, penalties and goalie changes only, with no coordinates. mjhl refuses the game-summary feed, so mjhl_game_summary returns empty event frames and mjhl_pbp returns plays without game metadata. Errors follow the package vocabulary: a 404 raises NoDataError, and any other unusable reply (HockeyTech reports most errors as an HTTP 200 with an error in the body) raises AssetFetchError.

Every league reports shot and event locations in x_coord / y_coord on one canvas: 600 by 300, origin at the top left, centre ice at (300, 150). The feed puts the home team's attack toward x = 0 and the visitor's toward x = 600 in every period. There is no other canvas, whatever the league. The play-by-play also carries derived frames, ported from fastRhockey's pwhl_pbp, all rotations of a centre-origin frame in feet (x from -100 to 100, y from -42.5 to 42.5): shots = pbp.filter(pl.col("x_coord").is_not_null()).select( "event", "team_id", "x_coord", "y_coord", "x_coord_right", "y_coord_right" ) print(shots.select(pl.col("x_coord").max(), pl.col("y_coord").max())) # never past 600 / 300 x_coord_right / y_coord_right (and the vertical pair) are null where the side is unknown, such as on a faceoff or in a game without its summary. See the league pages, such as ECHL and PWHL, for every function's parameters and Returns table.

Twenty-five international basketball families live under sportsdataverse.basketball.<home>. A home is named for a provider family, not always a league: some providers serve many competitions, and some leagues are served by a provider that also serves others. The international competitions ESPN covers are separate, in the ESPN league modules (fiba, olympics_mbk, olympics_wbk, nbl).

Two consequences of naming homes for providers: the function prefix is the provider's (sportpress_schedule in bnxt, sportality_pbp in dbl, nbl_rosetta_match_pbp in nbl_au), and one home can reach several competitions through a league or competition argument (scb_games(league="dbbl"), genius_competition_games(comp_id), atrium_fixtures(website_id)).

Most homes have a schedule or results, standings, box scores and play-by-play; many add shot charts, leaders and player pages. Each also exports its parsers (parse_<home>_*). The league pages list every function with its parameters and Returns table: EuroLeague, FIBA, Genius, Atrium, CEBL and the rest under Basketball in the sidebar.

Seasons are END years at the public API (season=2026 is 2025-26 for a winter league; a summer league's season is its calendar year). Each runtime maps it to the provider's own key. Polite pacing. Requests go through one throttled session that spaces them at least one second apart. Proxies are optional and named. A few providers block some networks; set GENIUS_PROXY or CBA_PROXY to route those families through a proxy. The value is never logged. Some sites need curl_cffi. Live FIBA game pages and P. LEAGUE+ sit behind bot protection, so their runtimes use curl_cffi (pip install curl_cffi, or the all extra). Tidy by default. Wrappers return a polars DataFrame; return_parsed=False gives the raw payload and return_as_pandas=True gives pandas. from sportsdataverse.basketball.cebl import cebl_games, cebl_standings from sportsdataverse.basketball.easl import easl_standings standings = cebl_standings(season=2025) # CEBL plays in summer: the 2025 season games = cebl_games(season=2025) east_asia = easl_standings(season=2026) # 2025-26 print(standings.height, games.height, east_asia.height) Several of these sources are unofficial uses of public sites, and some docstrings carry a release flag saying the data may be used for reference but not redistributed. Read the function's docstring before republishing anything.

sportsdataverse.odds wraps the public market-data APIs of two prediction markets, Polymarket and Kalshi, beside The Odds API's sportsbook lines. Both are read-only and keyless: the wrappers read events, markets, prices and order books. Trading and account endpoints need signed keys and are not wrapped.

Polymarket serves metadata and prices from two hosts, and the function names say which: The query parameters are passed as strings, as the API takes them. from sportsdataverse.odds import polymarket_gamma_events, polymarket_gamma_markets sports_events = polymarket_gamma_events(closed="false", limit="5", tag_slug="sports") busiest = polymarket_gamma_markets(closed="false", limit="5", order="volume24hr", ascending="false") print(sports_events.height, busiest.height)

Kalshi organizes markets as series (a market family, such as every NFL game), events (one game) and markets (one contract on that event). from sportsdataverse.odds import kalshi_events, kalshi_series_list sports_series = kalshi_series_list(category="Sports") nfl_games = kalshi_events(limit="5", series_ticker="KXNFLGAME", status="open") print(sports_series.height, nfl_games.height)

Wrappers return a polars DataFrame by default; return_parsed=False gives the raw JSON and return_as_pandas=True gives pandas. parse_polymarket and parse_kalshi parse a raw payload you already have. Errors follow the package vocabulary: a 404 raises NoDataError, a failed fetch AssetFetchError, a 400 / 422 ValueError. A market price is what a contract trades at, and the prices of the two sides need not sum to 1 (the bid-ask spread), so they are not de-vigged probabilities. To compare them with sportsbook lines or a model, the market helpers in sportsdataverse.wexp (prob_from_american, devig_multiplicative) put both on one scale. The Odds page lists every function with its parameters and Returns table.

Player, athlete, team and game ids are join keys, and a join is only as correct as the dtype agreement on its two sides. This page sets out which dtype each part of the package gives an id, where the exceptions are, and how to join safely.

The ESPN, NHL and HockeyTech parsers emit every id / *_id column as Int64. *_ids columns hold lists and are not ids. All three families go through one cast, _codegen_runtime._cast_ids_int64, which is conservative: A column is converted only when every non-null value survives the cast. A String column with a value that is not an integer is left as it came, and the parser warns SchemaDriftWarning naming the column, so nothing is silently nulled or corrupted. A float-origin id goes straight to Int64, never through text, so it can never come out as "123.0". Whitespace around a String id is stripped, and an empty string is null. An empty frame is cast too, so a result with no rows joins like one with rows. A few ids are text by design and stay String: ESPN's now_id ("1-44686270"), NHL stats-rest formatted_season_id and the country id, and NFL.com gsis player ids ("00-0034796"). With return_as_pandas=True the Int64 ids are pandas' nullable Int64, or int64[pyarrow] for the Arrow-backed frames. from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_game_rosters, espn_nba_scoreboard games = espn_nba_scoreboard(dates="20240317") roster = espn_nba_game_rosters(game_id=401585607) print({c: str(games.schema[c]) for c in ("game_id", "home_id", "away_id")}) print({c: str(roster.schema[c]) for c in ("athlete_id", "team_id", "game_id")}) # {'game_id': 'Int64', 'home_id': 'Int64', 'away_id': 'Int64'} # {'athlete_id': 'Int64', 'team_id': 'Int64', 'game_id': 'Int64'}
documents.s: The rule: Int64 at the parser boundary

documents.t: The load_* functions read parquet files published to GitHub releases, and they return the dtypes those files were written with. Some of those files still carry String ids while the live parsers now emit Int64: Joining one of those String columns to an Int64 column raises SchemaError. Cast the release side first. An Int32 id (such as team_id in those rosters, load_pwhl_rosters or load_pwhl_xg_pbp) joins an Int64 one as it is. Some loaders already canonicalize their ids to Int64 at the loader boundary (the CFB loaders, for example), so check the schema rather than assuming either way. import polars as pl from sportsdataverse.pwhl import load_pwhl_schedules, pwhl_schedule live = pwhl_schedule(season=2025) # HockeyTech parser: Int64 ids release = load_pwhl_schedules([2025]) # release file: String ids print(live.schema["game_id"], release.schema["game_id"]) # Int64 String release = release.with_columns(pl.col("game_id", "home_team_id", "away_team_id").cast(pl.Int64)) assert release.schema["game_id"] == live.schema["game_id"] both = live.join(release.select("game_id"), on="game_id", how="inner")
documents.s: Release loaders keep their published dtypes

documents.t: find_team, find_athlete and find_event return ESPN's own JSON record for the match, a dict with camelCase keys, so ["id"] is a string. Convert it with int() before you compare it to, or join it against, a parser frame. from sportsdataverse import find_event, find_team lakers = find_team("lakers", league="nba") event = find_event(date="2024-03-17", league="nba", home="Orlando") print(repr(lakers["id"]), repr(event["id"])) # '13' '401585607' team_id = int(lakers["id"]) game_id = int(event["id"])
documents.s: Name resolvers return raw ESPN strings

documents.t: Not yet covered by the Int64 rule: the soccer leagues' scoreboard, standings, summary, teams_site and team_roster wrappers, and the cricket leagues' scoreboard, standings and summary wrappers. Codegen routes those to the soccer and cricket parsers, which do not cast, so their ids are String. The same leagues' other wrappers (news, injuries, ...) go through the common ESPN parsers and are Int64. from sportsdataverse.soccer.epl import espn_epl_scoreboard epl = espn_epl_scoreboard(dates="20241026") print({c: str(epl.schema[c]) for c in ("event_id", "home_team_id", "away_team_id")}) # {'event_id': 'String', 'home_team_id': 'String', 'away_team_id': 'String'}
documents.s: Soccer and cricket ESPN wrappers are still String

documents.t: A wrapper called with raw=True or return_parsed=False hands back the provider's JSON, and some hand-written functions return dicts of lightly processed records. No cast happens there. espn_nba_pbp(game_id, return_parsed=False)["plays"], for example, is a list of dicts whose participants.0.athlete.id arrives as a string.
documents.s: Raw payloads are whatever the provider sent

documents.t: This joins one NBA game's shooting plays to its game roster, so each shot carries the shooter's name. The plays come from a raw payload (String ids), the roster from a parser (Int64 ids), so the id is cast once at the boundary and the dtypes are asserted before the join. import polars as pl from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_game_rosters, espn_nba_pbp game_id = 401585607 plays = pl.from_dicts(espn_nba_pbp(game_id=game_id, return_parsed=False)["plays"], infer_schema_length=None) roster = espn_nba_game_rosters(game_id=game_id) shots = plays.filter(pl.col("shootingPlay") == True).select( "game_play_number", "text", "scoringPlay", pl.col("participants.0.athlete.id").cast(pl.Int64).alias("athlete_id"), ) assert shots.schema["athlete_id"] == roster.schema["athlete_id"] == pl.Int64 shots = shots.join( roster.select("athlete_id", "athlete_display_name", "team_id"), on="athlete_id", how="left", validate="m:1", ) assert shots["athlete_display_name"].null_count() == 0 print(shots.group_by("athlete_display_name").agg(pl.len().alias("shots")).sort("shots", descending=True).head(3)) validate="m:1" makes polars raise if the roster has two rows for one athlete, and the null-count assertion catches a join that matched nothing, which is what a dtype mismatch hidden by a cast to text looks like.
documents.s: A worked join: shots to the game roster

documents.t: Pick one dtype per id and cast at the boundary, where the data enters your code, not in the middle of a pipeline. Assert before you join: assert left.schema[key] == right.schema[key]. Never cast an id to text to make a join line up. If you must have text, cast the integer (pl.col("id").cast(pl.Int64).cast(pl.String)), never a float, so you get "123" and not "123.0"; zero-padded source ids lose or gain leading zeros either way. Stored frames: if you persist parser output, keep the ids Int64 across every season. Concatenating an older String season with a new Int64 one through pl.concat(how="diagonal_relaxed") silently turns the column back into String. The migration guide has the producer checklist.

sportsdataverse-py supports Python 3.10 through 3.14 and runs on polars 2 (polars>=2.0,<3). polars 1.x is no longer supported. Every loader and wrapper returns a polars DataFrame by default, and most accept return_as_pandas=True if you want pandas instead.

pip install --pre sportsdataverse # 0.2.0b1, the 0.2.0 beta Without --pre, pip installs 0.1.4, the latest final release, until 0.2.0 ships. With uv, which the project uses day to day: uv add sportsdataverse # the latest commit on main, ahead of the next release uv add "sportsdataverse @ git+https://github.com/sportsdataverse/sportsdataverse-py" For a development checkout, clone the repository and sync every extra into the checkout's own .venv: git clone https://github.com/sportsdataverse/sportsdataverse-py.git cd sportsdataverse-py uv sync --all-extras uv run pytest CONTRIBUTING.md in the repository covers the rest of the contributor workflow (lint, type checks, live-test gates, changelog fragments).

The extras are defined in [project.optional-dependencies] in pyproject.toml. None of them is needed for the core loaders and ESPN wrappers. Three notes on the extras: [all] leaves out mcp. Install sportsdataverse[all,mcp] to get both. sportypy is GPL-3.0. sportsdataverse-py is MIT and never bundles it; the extra installs it beside the package, so check that the GPL fits your project before you depend on it. sdvplot is MIT. curl_cffi is in tests and all only. The stats.nba.com / stats.wnba.com wrappers need it for live calls, as do a few international basketball sites. If it is missing, those calls raise an ImportError that names it (pip install curl_cffi). See Troubleshooting. The sdvplot extra installs sdvplot[mpl], so matplotlib comes with it. For another backend, add sdvplot's own extra: pip install "sdvplot[plotly]" or "sdvplot[altair]".

Installing the package puts an sdv console script on your path. It resolves names to ESPN ids, searches the function index and controls the package-wide HTTP response cache, without writing any Python. On a terminal it prints styled cards and tables (team cards in the team's own colours, tables sized to the window); piped or with NO_COLOR set, the output is plain. The --json flag prints JSON for piping to jq; put it before the subcommand (sdv --json find-team ...), which both CLIs below accept. The new CLI also takes it after the subcommand. sdv --help and sdv <command> --help list every command and option. The CLI is built on cyclopts and Rich and needs Python 3.11 or newer. On Python 3.10, or in an environment without cyclopts or Rich, sdv runs the classic CLI instead: the same commands, flags, --json output and exit codes, in plain text. The conda package needs Python 3.11 or newer and always installs the new CLI. The --league choices for the find-* commands are nba, wnba, mbb, wbb, cfb, nfl, mlb and nhl. list-functions and function-count take any league or provider group the package has, such as euroleague or pwhl. sdv find-team lakers --league nba # a card: id 13, LAL, colours, clubhouse link sdv find-team "Lakres" -l nba # no match: exit 1, with "did you mean Los Angeles Lakers?" sdv --json find-event 2025-02-09 -l nfl # {"id": "401671889", ... "Kansas City Chiefs at Philadelphia Eagles"} sdv list-functions -l nba -s roster # espn_nba_game_rosters, espn_nba_team_roster, ... sdv cache stats # mode off · entries 0 · disk bytes 0 B Exit codes: 0 when the command succeeded (for find-*, a match was found), 1 when a find-* command found no match, and 2 on an error, printed as sdv: <message> on stderr, or a usage error such as a missing --league. An error covers invalid input, a host that answered "nothing there" (NoDataError) and a fetch that failed (AssetFetchError). The cache commands control the response cache that the package's HTTP layer checks before going to the network (sportsdataverse.cache; it is off by default). That cache is separate from the NFL loaders' cache, which the NFL cache recipe covers.

sdv-docs is a Model Context Protocol server that lets an AI assistant search this documentation: the function reference, the Returns tables, the endpoint metadata and the R packages' indexes. It needs the mcp extra: pip install "sportsdataverse[mcp]>=0.2.0b1" # 0.1.4 has no sdv-docs; the pin upgrades it sdv-docs --version With no arguments sdv-docs serves its tools over stdio, so you register it with your MCP client as a command (sdv-docs). It exposes six tools: search, get_function, find_columns, find_endpoints, list_datasets and index_info. The server never imports sportsdataverse itself, so it starts in about a second. It reads a prebuilt SQLite index, downloaded on first use from the docs-index release of the repository, cached locally and re-checked at most once a day. Set SDV_DOCS_DB to the path of an index file to use that file and never download.

0.2.0 is the release after 0.1.4 (0.1.5 was never published; its changes ship in 0.2.0); it ships first as the 0.2.0b1 pre-release (pip install --pre sportsdataverse). It carries seventeen breaking changes, each recorded as a changelog.d/*.breaking.md fragment; the changes are on main already. This page takes them one at a time: what changed, who is affected, a before/after snippet and how to migrate. The fragments are the source of record, and the release's CHANGELOG.md section is built from them. Most code is affected by at most two of them: the Int64 ids and the polars 2 floor. Read those first. In the snippets, # 0.1.x marks code that shows the old behaviour (it is not meant to be run against 0.2.0) and # 0.2.0 marks the replacement.

What changed. The ESPN, NHL and HockeyTech parsers emit every id / *_id column as Int64. Those columns used to be String, Int32, or Float64 where a missing value passed through pandas. This covers the generated espn_<lg>_<short> wrappers, the hand-written espn_<lg>_schedule / espn_<lg>_teams / espn_<lg>_game_rosters, the ESPN injury and depth-chart snapshots, the ESPN content parser, the NCAA ESPN crosswalks, the NFL processor (*_player_id, pos_team and its lags and leads), the NHL API parsers, nhl_player_props / pwhl_player_props, and every HockeyTech frame (PWHL and the 19 other leagues). With return_as_pandas=True the same columns are pandas' nullable Int64 (or int64[pyarrow] for the Arrow-backed frames). A few ids are text by design and stay String: ESPN's now_id, NHL stats-rest formatted_season_id, and NFL.com gsis ids such as "00-0034796". An id column holding a value that is not an integer keeps its dtype and warns SchemaDriftWarning. Not yet covered: the soccer leagues' scoreboard, standings, summary, teams_site and team_roster wrappers and the cricket leagues' scoreboard, standings and summary wrappers keep String ids in this release. Who is affected. Anyone who compares an id to a string, joins a parser frame to a String id, or stores these frames. # 0.1.x props.filter(pl.col("player_id") == "8478402") # 0.2.0 import polars as pl from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_scoreboard games = espn_nba_scoreboard(dates="20240317") print(games.schema["game_id"]) # Int64 games.filter(pl.col("home_id") == 19) # compare to an int, not "19" How to migrate. Compare ids to ints. If you need text, cast back with pl.col("team_id").cast(pl.String) (pandas: .astype("string")); an Int64 id stringifies as "123", never "123.0". Release loaders keep their published dtypes. Several release files still carry String ids: load_pwhl_schedules (game_id, home_team_id, away_team_id), load_pwhl_pbp (team_id, player_team_id, home_team_id, away_team_id, game_season_id), the PWHL box scores' player_id, load_{mbb,nba,wbb,wnba}_rosters (athlete_id, position_id, status_id) and load_{mbb,nba,wnba}_game_rosters (game_id). Joining one of those to live parser output raises SchemaError, so cast first: release.with_columns(pl.col("game_id").cast(pl.Int64)). An Int32 id joins an Int64 one as it is. IDs and joins has a worked example. build_nfl_season cache: PIPELINE_VERSION is 2, so per-game frames cached by an earlier version are rebuilt rather than mixed into a season with the new Int64 ids. Nothing to do. Producers that store or republish these frames should move the published ids to Int64 now, not back to String, and rewrite the stored history in one pass: Deploy order: update (or pin) every producer that writes these frames first, then upgrade. Stored history: cast the stored ids once (pl.col(c).cast(pl.Int64)) or rebuild every season before the first post-upgrade run. Otherwise pd.concat / to_parquet of the master fails on a mixed column, and pl.concat(how="diagonal_relaxed") silently turns the ids back into String. RDS: pyreadr.write_rds cannot write a nullable Int64 with a missing value. For that write only, cast the id columns to pandas' nullable Int32 when every id fits in 32 bits (df[id_cols] = df[id_cols].astype("Int32")), otherwise to float64. The parquet stays Int64. R packages: releases rebuilt from these parsers carry integer ids where hoopR, wehoop and fastRhockey document some of them as character. Republish every season in the same pass and update the R documentation.
documents.s: Ids are Int64 at the parser boundary

documents.t: What changed. The runtime pin is polars>=2.0,<3. polars 1.x is no longer supported, and the package may use 2.x-only API. Who is affected. Environments that pin polars below 2. # 0.1.x pip install "sportsdataverse" "polars<2" # 0.2.0 pip install -U "sportsdataverse" "polars>=2,<3" How to migrate. Upgrade polars, then check your own code against the polars 2 upgrade guide. The changes that bite most often: explode() turns an empty list into zero rows (pass empty_as_null= explicitly), casting a String column with .cast(pl.Date) raises (use str.to_date()), is_in raises on an Int column against a float list, and pl.read_parquet on a GitHub release URL fails with HTTP 501 (pass use_pyarrow=True).

What changed. In espn_{nba,wnba,mbb,wbb}_pbp plays, coordinate.x / coordinate.y keep their names but change meaning and dtype. They were ESPN's raw feet (hoop at (25, 0)); they are now the full-court frame the hoopR / wehoop files use (x = y - 41.75, y = x - 25, both negated on home-team plays), always Float64. ESPN's values move to coordinate.x.raw / coordinate.y.raw (coordinate_x_raw / coordinate_y_raw once snake-cased). On the NBA / WNBA free throws that hoopR / wehoop's "Free Throw" match finds, the raw pair holds the pinned (25, 13.75), as in the published files. The release converters (helper_<lg>_play_by_play) rebuild from the raw pair, so a processed payload converts once. Who is affected. Shot charts and anything that reads coordinate.x / coordinate.y as ESPN feet. # 0.1.x: ESPN feet shots = plays.filter(pl.col("shootingPlay") == True).select("coordinate.x", "coordinate.y") # 0.2.0: ESPN feet are the .raw pair; filter out the missing-location sentinel import polars as pl from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_pbp, nba_game_page plays = pl.from_dicts(espn_nba_pbp(game_id=401585607, return_parsed=False)["plays"], infer_schema_length=None) shots = plays.filter( (pl.col("shootingPlay") == True) & (pl.col("coordinate.x.raw") > nba_game_page.COORD_SENTINEL) ).select("coordinate.x.raw", "coordinate.y.raw", "coordinate.x", "coordinate.y") How to migrate. Read the .raw pair where you wanted ESPN feet, or use the new columns directly if you were converting to the hoopR frame yourself. ESPN's missing-location sentinel reads about ±2.1e8 after the transform; filter on coordinate_x_raw > nba_game_page.COORD_SENTINEL (the snake-cased name in the processed frames).
documents.s: Basketball pbp coordinates use the hoopR / wehoop frame

documents.t: What changed. espn_<league>_leaders() returns one row per athlete and stat category (#1018). It used to return a single envelope row whose pagination_*, league_* and current_season_* columns described the request, with the athletes packed into one cell. Leagues without a leaderboard return zero rows. Who is affected. Callers that read the envelope columns, or that unpacked the athletes / categories cells themselves. # 0.2.0 from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_leaders leaders = espn_nba_leaders() # one row per athlete raw = espn_nba_leaders(return_parsed=False) # pagination and per-stat ranks How to migrate. Drop the unpacking step. Read page counts and ESPN's per-stat ranks from return_parsed=False.
documents.s: ESPN leaders return one row per athlete

documents.t: What changed. espn_<lg>_game_rosters(raw=True) (mbb, wbb, nba, wnba, nfl, nhl, cfb) returns the Core v2 competitors payload, a dict. raw= used to be accepted and ignored, so it returned the parsed frame. Who is affected. Callers that passed raw=True and used the result as a frame. # 0.1.x: raw=True returned the frame anyway roster = espn_nba_game_rosters(game_id=401585607, raw=True) # 0.2.0 from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_game_rosters roster = espn_nba_game_rosters(game_id=401585607) # the parsed frame payload = espn_nba_game_rosters(game_id=401585607, raw=True) # the raw dict How to migrate. Drop raw=True where you want the frame.

What changed. espn_mbb_pbp(), espn_nba_pbp(), espn_wbb_pbp() and espn_wnba_pbp() return the play-by-play frame the release publishes, the one load_<lg>_pbp() reads: snake_case columns, Int32 team / athlete / game ids, the Int64 play id, game_date, the hoopR / wehoop shot coordinates, athlete_name_{1,2,3}, the rebuilt running score with score_source, columns in the release's order, and a zero-row frame with the release's columns for a game with no play-by-play (playByPlaySource == "none") or 10 or fewer plays. They used to return a dict whose plays were dotted camelCase records with String ids. The dict is still there with return_parsed=False, and raw=True is unchanged. The WBB release's season-level win-probability columns are not added per game. Who is affected. Callers that index the result (["plays"], ["boxscore"], ...) or pass it to game_page_frames() or a helper_<lg>_play_by_play / _team_box / _player_box converter. # 0.1.x plays = pl.from_dicts(espn_mbb_pbp(game_id=401638637)["plays"], infer_schema_length=None) # 0.2.0 from sportsdataverse.mbb import espn_mbb_pbp plays = espn_mbb_pbp(game_id=401638637) # the release frame game = espn_mbb_pbp(game_id=401638637, return_parsed=False) # the dict from sportsdataverse.wnba import espn_wnba_pbp plays = espn_wnba_pbp(game_id=401620238) # same for WBB / WNBA How to migrate. Use the frame's snake_case columns, or add return_parsed=False where you want the dict.
documents.s: ESPN MBB / NBA / WBB / WNBA pbp return the release frame

documents.t: What changed. The six schedule copies that sent seasonType (NFL, NHL, WNBA, NBA, MBB, WBB) now send seasontype. ESPN ignored the camelCase key, so season_type= with dates=YYYY&week=N never filtered; it does now. Who is affected. Callers passing season_type= to those schedules. The same call returns different rows: only that season type. # 0.2.0: season_type=2 now really returns the regular season only from sportsdataverse.nfl import espn_nfl_schedule week1 = espn_nfl_schedule(dates=2024, week=1, season_type=2) How to migrate. If you relied on the unfiltered rows, drop season_type=.
documents.s: ESPN schedules filter by season type

documents.t: What changed. In fox_nfl_pbp / fox_cfb_pbp, play_team is the club code of the drive group the play is filed under (for example "NYG"). It used to hold the name of the player Fox credits the play to, which moves to the new play_player column. Who is affected. Anyone reading play_team from the Fox pbp. # 0.1.x: play_team held a player name pbp.select("play_team") # 0.2.0 from sportsdataverse.nfl import fox_nfl_pbp pbp = fox_nfl_pbp("11052") # a Fox Bifrost event id pbp.select("play_team", "play_player") # club code ("BUF"), credited player How to migrate. Rename your play_team reads to play_player where you meant the player.
documents.s: Fox pbp splits the team from the player

documents.t: What changed. Two helpers no longer hide a failure: nfl_players_crosswalk() raises AssetFetchError when the nflverse players master cannot be fetched. It used to return a zero-row frame, which nulled every id in a join. An absent asset still gives zero rows, and a failed DynastyProcess load now warns (the yahoo / cbs ids are null). nfl.update_config(cache_mode=...) raises ValueError for a mode other than "memory", "filesystem" or "off". An unknown mode used to switch caching off silently. Who is affected. Pipelines that called either and relied on the silent fallback. # 0.1.x: "disk" switched the cache off without a word update_config(cache_mode="disk") # 0.2.0 from sportsdataverse.errors import AssetFetchError from sportsdataverse.nfl import nfl_players_crosswalk, update_config update_config(cache_mode="filesystem") # "memory", "filesystem" or "off"; anything else raises ValueError try: xwalk = nfl_players_crosswalk() except AssetFetchError: xwalk = None # the fetch failed: retry later, do not join on nulls How to migrate. Catch AssetFetchError where you can retry, and fix any cache mode string that was not one of the three.

What changed. The stats.ncaa.org fetch layer raises NoDataError on a real 404 after one request, and AssetFetchError (naming which) for a banned or exhausted proxy pool, an uncleared bm-verify challenge or the Terms gate. Both used to be RuntimeError. A missing proxy configuration is still RuntimeError. Who is affected. Code that caught RuntimeError around stats.ncaa.org calls. # 0.1.x (not run here: stats.ncaa.org bans cloud IPs) try: pbp = ncaa_mbb_play_by_play([5254137]) except RuntimeError: ... # 0.2.0 (not run here: stats.ncaa.org bans cloud IPs) from sportsdataverse.errors import AssetFetchError, NoDataError from sportsdataverse.mbb import ncaa_mbb_play_by_play try: pbp = ncaa_mbb_play_by_play([5254137]) except NoDataError: pbp = None # the game page does not exist except AssetFetchError: raise # banned, challenged or out of proxies: the answer is unknown How to migrate. Catch AssetFetchError (and NoDataError where a missing page is expected) instead of RuntimeError.
documents.s: stats.ncaa.org failures raise the shared vocabulary

documents.t: What changed. ncaa_{mbb,wbb}_play_by_play and ncaa_{mbb,wbb}_box_scores raise AssetFetchError when a fetch fails (a ban, an exhausted pool, an uncleared challenge) instead of dropping that game, which made a ban read as a smaller season. errors="skip" keeps going and adds a scrape_status column with one row per dropped game saying why. Who is affected. Season scrapes that expected a partial frame on failure. # 0.2.0 (not run here: stats.ncaa.org bans cloud IPs) import polars as pl from sportsdataverse.mbb import ncaa_mbb_box_scores box = ncaa_mbb_box_scores([5254137, 5254138], errors="skip") dropped = box.filter(pl.col("scrape_status").is_not_null()) How to migrate. Pass errors="skip" and read scrape_status if you want the old keep-going behaviour, with the drops now visible.
documents.s: NCAA basketball scrapes raise instead of dropping games

documents.t: What changed. Processed NFL and CFB plays keep the documented Float64 for the EP/WP family, first_down_prob, prob_2pt and drive_start; they were Float32 when a model scored. No value changes. NFL teamParticipants has one struct field order, and create_box_score(plays_frame) still reproduces advBoxScore exactly. Who is affected. Code that asserted Float32 on those columns or concatenated them with frames written by an earlier version. # 0.2.0 import polars as pl from sportsdataverse.nfl import build_nfl_season plays = build_nfl_season(game_ids=[401671889]) print(plays.schema["home_wp_before"]) # Float64 How to migrate. Cast stored Float32 history to Float64 before concatenating it with new frames.
documents.s: NFL and CFB processed plays keep their documented Float64

documents.t: What changed. sportsdataverse.nfl.model_vars.qbr_vars is in the QBR trainer's order (qbr_epa, pass_epa, rush_epa, sack_epa, pen_epa, spread), and nfl/models/qbr_model.ubj is re-saved with those feature names (same trees). A frame in the old column order raises instead of scoring permuted inputs. Who is affected. Code that scores the bundled QBR model directly. # 0.2.0 from sportsdataverse.nfl.model_vars import qbr_vars print(qbr_vars) # ['qbr_epa', 'pass_epa', 'rush_epa', 'sack_epa', 'pen_epa', 'spread'] How to migrate. Select features with qbr_vars (frame.select(qbr_vars)) rather than a hand-written column list.
documents.s: The NFL QBR model checks its feature order

documents.t: What changed. The current season flips on the Wednesday after Labor Day, and week 1 starts on the Thursday after it (nflreadr's rules). Earlier code read the week one high in 2015-16, 2020-22 and 2026-27. most_recent_nfl_season and get_current_week are now that one rule, so from September 1 to that Wednesday they give the previous season (week 22), not the new one. Who is affected. Jobs that run in early September and default to the current season. # 0.2.0 from sportsdataverse.nfl import get_current_week, most_recent_nfl_season print(most_recent_nfl_season(), get_current_week()) How to migrate. Pass the season explicitly in jobs that run between September 1 and the Wednesday after Labor Day.
documents.s: The current NFL season follows nflreadr's rule

documents.t: What changed. Columns whose values are codes, not numbers, keep their text: Basketball-Reference: bref_team_roster() returns number as String (was Float64), so Robert Parish's "00" is no longer 0.0. Bart Torvik: torvik_player_stats() / parse_torvik_player_stats() return number as String (was Int64), so the "00" jerseys no longer merge into the 0 rows. 247Sports site pages: primary_color, jersey and postal_code are String (were Int64 when every value was digits); a (0, 0) latitude / longitude pair, 247's no-location sentinel, is null. KenPom: the jersey column is String on every page and renamed to jersey (column_0 on the team pages, column_0_rk on the box pages). Who is affected. Code that does arithmetic on jerseys or reads the old KenPom column names. # 0.1.x kenpom_team.select("column_0") # 0.2.0 (not run here: the KenPom pages need a subscription login) kenpom_team.select("jersey") How to migrate. Treat jerseys as text, and rename the KenPom column reads.
documents.s: Provider jerseys and padded codes stay String

documents.t: What changed. pwhl_player_box(game_id) returns {"skaters": DataFrame, "goalies": DataFrame}, as fastRhockey's pwhl_player_box does. It used to return a single DataFrame, which was always empty. Who is affected. Every caller of pwhl_player_box. # 0.1.x box = pwhl_player_box(game_id) # one (empty) frame # 0.2.0 from sportsdataverse.pwhl import pwhl_player_box, pwhl_schedule game_id = int(pwhl_schedule(season=2025)["game_id"][0]) box = pwhl_player_box(game_id) skaters, goalies = box["skaters"], box["goalies"] How to migrate. Index the result by "skaters" or "goalies".
documents.s: PWHL player box returns skaters and goalies

documents.t: What changed. build_spring_football_pbp(..., league="cfl") and enrich_spring_football_pbp(..., league="cfl") raise ValueError. They used to score CFL plays with the NFL EP/WP boosters, whose support is yardline_100 1-99 while a CFL field is 110 yards with three downs. No CFL pipeline ships. get_sf_constants("cfl") still returns the descriptive CFL rule constants. Who is affected. Anyone who built CFL EP/WP through these functions. Those numbers were not meaningful. # 0.2.0 from sportsdataverse.football.spring_football_constants import get_sf_constants cfl = get_sf_constants("cfl") # the rule constants still work How to migrate. Drop CFL from spring-football EP/WP runs. The UFL and XFL are unchanged.
documents.s: Spring football EP/WP refuses the CFL

documents.t: Nothing deprecated in 0.2.0 breaks yet. Each name below still works, warns DeprecationWarning naming its replacement, and is removed in 0.4.0, two minor releases on: the old package paths moved under sportsdataverse.basketball, sportsdataverse.providers and sportsdataverse.analytics; the 12 old *_espn_ext names of the wrappers renamed to *_site; 29 unread sportsdataverse.config release URLs; dl_utils.ESPNHTTP / ESPNResponse, the df.janitor case methods and decorators.record_mem_usage / record_time_usage; espn_<lg>_teams.cache_clear() and sportsdataverse.scrape.ncaa.league_config; pwhl_team_ratings(league=...); the load_nba_stats_*_v3 and four load_wnba_stats_* loader shims. How to migrate. Run your code with python -W error::DeprecationWarning (or pytest -W error::DeprecationWarning) and follow each message.

Beyond fetching and tidying data, sdv-py ships the models that turn football play-by-play into expected points and win probability, a validator that checks a processed game against invariant rules, a win-expectancy benchmarking harness, and a set of season analytics built on the released play-by-play. Every bundled model and fitted constant names the script that produced it on the Model lineage page.

sportsdataverse/nfl/ep_wp.py is the one place NFL models are applied and EPA / WPA are derived. Construction code (the ESPN processor, the Shield rebuild, load_nfl_pbp) builds a frame; ep_wp scores it. enrich_nfl_pbp(df) scores an nflverse-shape frame in nflfastR's order: EP, EPA, WP, WPA, CP and CPOE, then xYAC. The default and only implemented method="lead_diff" ports nflfastR's helper_add_ep_wp.R: it scores one start-of-play ep, derives epa / wpa with lead differences grouped by game_id (so concatenated games never leak into each other), applies nflfastR's scoring, end-of-half and overtime overlays, and substitutes kickoff features (the season's touchback yard line, first and ten) before scoring. Against nflverse's own columns the correlations are about 0.996 for ep, 0.994 for epa, 0.997 for wp and 0.998 for vegas_wp; wpa sits near 0.89, which is the WP model's per-play noise amplified by differencing, not a derivation error. import polars as pl from sportsdataverse.nfl import load_nfl_pbp from sportsdataverse.nfl.ep_wp import enrich_nfl_pbp pbp = load_nfl_pbp([2024]) scored = enrich_nfl_pbp(pbp) # about a minute for a season print(scored.select("game_id", "play_id", "ep", "epa", "wp", "wpa", "cpoe").drop_nulls("epa").head(3)) The bundled NFL boosters (sportsdataverse/nfl/models/*.ubj) are the EP, naive and spread WP, and CP models from the nfl_model_artifacts release, plus field-goal, QBR, two-point, expected-pass and punt models; the fourth-down decision surface lives in sportsdataverse/nfl/nfl_fourth_down.py. A missing model warns once and nulls its columns; enrich_nfl_pbp(df, strict=True) or SDV_PY_MODELS_STRICT=1 raises instead, for producers that must not publish nulls. The ESPN path (NFLPlayProcess, build_nfl_season(game_ids=...)) shares the same EPA / WPA derivation (calculate_epa / calculate_wpa), so both paths produce the same numbers from the same inputs.
documents.s: NFL expected points and win probability

documents.t: sportsdataverse/cfb/models/ ships rule-era XGBoost models trained in cfbfastR-cfb-data: expected points, naive and spread win probability, completion probability (with and without air yards), field goal, fourth down, two-point, expected pass, QBR and an overtime reach model. CFBPlayProcess.run_processing_pipeline() applies them, along with the fourth-down, field-goal and two-point decision surfaces, which are on by default. Each CFB booster ships a .card.json beside it with its training frame and seasons. from sportsdataverse.cfb import CFBPlayProcess game = CFBPlayProcess(gameId=401628334) game.espn_cfb_pbp() game.run_processing_pipeline() print(game.plays_frame.select("game_play_number", "EPA", "wp_before", "home_wp_before").tail(3))

sportsdataverse.validation.validate_game checks one processed NFL or CFB game against the packaged invariant rules, grouped by what they check (down, yards to go, possession, score, period, timeouts, play type, flags, win probability, the plays themselves and the box score), each scoped to the rule eras it applies to. It is pure and offline: nothing is fetched or written, and a rule whose columns the frame lacks is skipped rather than failed. It returns a GameReport. from sportsdataverse.validation import validate_game report = validate_game(game.plays_frame, "cfb") print(report.ok, len(report.errors), len(report.warnings)) print(report.counts_by_rule) report.ok is True when no rule fired at error severity. errors and warnings list the findings; counts_by_rule counts violations per rule whatever their severity; not_applicable names the rules the source cannot support. For a source that names columns differently (source= other than "espn"), SOURCE_COLUMNS supplies the ESPN-shaped aliases.

sportsdataverse.wexp is a harness for building and benchmarking pregame win probability models against the betting market. It has: Market oracles: nfl_market_oracle_from_schedule and build_nfl_market_oracle / build_cfb_market_oracle turn closing lines into a per-game frame with the market's home win probability. Market helpers: prob_from_american, prob_from_decimal, devig_multiplicative, devig_shin, spread_to_prob, logit_blend. Engines: margin Elo (elo_ratings, elo_predictor), Glickman-Stern (glickman_stern_predictor), rating predictors and vintage-based feature stores. A walk-forward backtest, run_backtest(oracle, predictor, model_id=...): each week the engine sees only games completed earlier in the walk, and the predictions are scored per season and pooled. Scoring: brier_score, log_loss_score, winner_accuracy, ece, calibration_table, closing_line_value, and score_baselines for the market and naive baselines. from sportsdataverse.nfl import load_nfl_schedule from sportsdataverse.wexp import elo_predictor, nfl_market_oracle_from_schedule, run_backtest oracle = nfl_market_oracle_from_schedule(load_nfl_schedule([2022, 2023])) probs, rows = run_backtest(oracle, elo_predictor(), model_id="elo") print(rows.filter(pl.col("season") == -1).select("metric", "value", "n")) # pooled: brier, log_loss, ... from sportsdataverse.wexp import devig_multiplicative, prob_from_american, spread_to_prob raw = [prob_from_american(-150), prob_from_american(130)] print(devig_multiplicative(raw)) # the two sides' no-vig probabilities print(spread_to_prob(7.0, sigma=13.45)) # a 7-point home favourite

Four modules turn released play-by-play into season-level tables. Each declares the columns it reads as a constant, so you can load only those. The football functions take CFB or NFL; shot_events / shot_attempts take NBA or WNBA stats shots. from sportsdataverse.cfb import load_cfb_pbp, load_cfb_rosters from sportsdataverse.analytics.paper_index import PBP_COLUMNS, deserved_wins, paper_index_games cfb_pbp = load_cfb_pbp(2024) games = paper_index_games(cfb_pbp.select(PBP_COLUMNS), "cfb") luck = deserved_wins(games).sort("luck_wins") # deserved_wins, luck_wins, luck_z per team print(luck.head(3)) from sportsdataverse.analytics.metric_curves import FOOTBALL_ATTEMPT_COLUMNS, football_attempts, metric_curves curves = metric_curves(football_attempts(cfb_pbp.select(FOOTBALL_ATTEMPT_COLUMNS)), "cfb") print( curves.filter((pl.col("entity_type") == "league") & (pl.col("metric") == "fg_pct_by_distance")).select( "x_lo", "x_hi", "attempts", "rate" ) ) from sportsdataverse.analytics.defense_vs_position import PBP_COLUMNS as DVP_COLUMNS from sportsdataverse.analytics.defense_vs_position import defense_vs_position dvp = defense_vs_position(cfb_pbp.select(DVP_COLUMNS["cfb"]), load_cfb_rosters(2024), "cfb") print( dvp.filter((pl.col("position_group") == "TE") & (pl.col("qualified") == True)) .sort("epa_per_play_allowed") .select("team_id", "plays", "epa_per_play_allowed") .head(3) ) Import from the modules themselves (from sportsdataverse.analytics.paper_index import ...): the top-level sportsdataverse namespace binds rolling_windows, metric_curves and defense_vs_position to the functions of the same name, not the modules. Paper Index is the model behind Game on Paper's deserved-win numbers; its fitted weights and fitting script are listed on the Model lineage page.
documents.s: Season analytics on the released play-by-play

documents.t: Short, complete recipes for the tasks people ask about most. Each block runs as written against the live sources; later blocks in a section reuse names from the earlier ones.

Join on ids, never on names, and check the dtypes on both sides first. The IDs and joins page explains which dtype each source uses. College football. The released CFB play-by-play and rosters both carry ESPN athlete ids as Int64. A roster has one row per team and athlete per season, so keep one row per (season, athlete_id) before joining. import polars as pl from sportsdataverse.cfb import load_cfb_pbp, load_cfb_rosters pbp = load_cfb_pbp(2024) rosters = load_cfb_rosters(2024).unique(["season", "athlete_id"], keep="first") passers = rosters.select( "season", pl.col("athlete_id").alias("passer_player_id"), pl.col("athlete_display_name").alias("passer"), pl.col("position_abbreviation").alias("passer_position"), ) assert pbp.schema["passer_player_id"] == passers.schema["passer_player_id"] dropbacks = pbp.filter(pl.col("pass") == True).join( passers, on=["season", "passer_player_id"], how="left", validate="m:1" ) print( dropbacks.group_by("passer", "pos_team") .agg(pl.len().alias("dropbacks"), pl.col("EPA").mean().alias("epa_per_dropback")) .filter(pl.col("dropbacks") >= 300) .sort("epa_per_dropback", descending=True) .head(5) ) NFL. nflverse play-by-play and rosters key players on the gsis id, which is text by design ("00-0034796"), so both sides are String and join as they are. from sportsdataverse.nfl import load_nfl_pbp, load_nfl_rosters nfl_pbp = load_nfl_pbp([2024]) nfl_rosters = load_nfl_rosters([2024]).unique(["season", "gsis_id"], keep="first") receivers = nfl_rosters.select( "season", pl.col("gsis_id").alias("receiver_player_id"), pl.col("position").alias("receiver_position"), ) assert nfl_pbp.schema["receiver_player_id"] == receivers.schema["receiver_player_id"] targets = nfl_pbp.filter(pl.col("receiver_player_id").is_not_null()).join( receivers, on=["season", "receiver_player_id"], how="left", validate="m:1" ) print(targets.group_by("receiver_position").agg(pl.col("epa").mean(), pl.len()).sort("len", descending=True)) nflverse rosters also carry espn_id, as String. To join them to ESPN-sourced frames, whose ids are Int64, cast it first: pl.col("espn_id").cast(pl.Int64, strict=False).
documents.s: Join play-by-play to rosters by id

documents.t: The quickest season of EPA is the nflverse play-by-play release, which already carries nflfastR's epa, wpa and the rest. team_epa = ( nfl_pbp.filter(pl.col("pass") == 1) .group_by("posteam") .agg(pl.col("epa").mean().alias("epa_per_dropback"), pl.len().alias("plays")) .sort("epa_per_dropback", descending=True) ) print(team_epa.head(5))

enrich_nfl_pbp re-scores an nflverse-shape frame with the models bundled in the package, in nflfastR's order: EP, EPA, WP, WPA, CP, CPOE and xYAC. The default method="lead_diff" is a port of nflfastR's helper_add_ep_wp.R. It is the way to score frames the release does not cover, such as a season rebuilt from NFL.com Shield JSON with build_nfl_season(seasons=[...], source="shield", raw_dir=...). A full season takes about a minute. from sportsdataverse.nfl.ep_wp import enrich_nfl_pbp scored = enrich_nfl_pbp(nfl_pbp) both = pl.DataFrame({"nflverse": nfl_pbp["epa"], "sdv": scored["epa"]}).drop_nulls() print(both.select(pl.corr("nflverse", "sdv"))) # about 0.99 Pass strict=True (or set SDV_PY_MODELS_STRICT=1) to raise when a model file is missing instead of nulling its columns.
documents.s: NFL scored by sdv-py's own models

documents.t: build_nfl_season with source="espn" (the default) processes ESPN games one by one through NFLPlayProcess, caches each processed game, and concatenates them. A game that fails is logged and skipped. The ESPN frame uses ESPN-style names: EPA, wpa, home_wp_before, and pos_team as an Int64 team id. from sportsdataverse import find_event from sportsdataverse.nfl import build_nfl_season super_bowl = int(find_event(date="20250209", league="nfl")["id"]) espn_plays = build_nfl_season(game_ids=[super_bowl]) print(espn_plays.group_by("pos_team").agg(pl.col("EPA").mean()))

The released CFB play-by-play carries EPA and WP for every game of a season. For a single game, or one the release does not hold yet, process it with CFBPlayProcess. cfb_team_epa = ( pbp.filter(pl.col("scrimmage_play") == True) .group_by("pos_team") .agg(pl.col("EPA").mean().alias("epa_per_play"), pl.len().alias("plays")) .filter(pl.col("plays") >= 500) .sort("epa_per_play", descending=True) ) print(cfb_team_epa.head(5)) from sportsdataverse.cfb import CFBPlayProcess game = CFBPlayProcess(gameId=401628334) game.espn_cfb_pbp() game.run_processing_pipeline() plays = game.plays_frame # one row per play, with EPA, wp_before, ... print(plays.select("game_play_number", "pos_team", "EPA", "home_wp_before").tail(3))

ESPN-processed games carry home_wp_before, the home side's win probability before each play. You need matplotlib (pip install matplotlib; the sdvplot and sportypy extras also install it). import matplotlib.pyplot as plt wp = espn_plays.select("game_play_number", "home_wp_before", "homeTeamAbbrev", "awayTeamAbbrev").drop_nulls( "home_wp_before" ) home, away = wp["homeTeamAbbrev"][0], wp["awayTeamAbbrev"][0] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4)) ax.plot(wp["game_play_number"], wp["home_wp_before"], color="black") ax.axhline(0.5, color="grey", linewidth=0.8, linestyle="--") ax.set_ylim(0, 1) ax.set_xlabel("Play number") ax.set_ylabel(f"{home} win probability") ax.set_title(f"{away} at {home}") fig.savefig("wp.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight") With sdvplot (pip install --pre "sportsdataverse[sdvplot]"), the same chart takes each side's team color. sdvplot.team_colors resolves abbreviations, ESPN ids or names to hex colors. import sdvplot home_color, away_color = sdvplot.team_colors("nfl", [home, away]) x, y = wp["game_play_number"].to_numpy(), wp["home_wp_before"].to_numpy() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4)) ax.fill_between(x, 0.5, y, where=y >= 0.5, interpolate=True, color=home_color, label=home) ax.fill_between(x, 0.5, y, where=y < 0.5, interpolate=True, color=away_color, label=away) ax.set_ylim(0, 1) ax.set_xlabel("Play number") ax.set_ylabel(f"{home} win probability") ax.legend(loc="upper left") fig.savefig("wp_team_colors.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight") sdvplot.matplotlib also has add_logos and title_image to put team logos on the axes or in the title.

The load_nfl_* loaders share one cache and one configuration (an NflConfig). There are three cache modes: from sportsdataverse.nfl import clear_cache, get_config, reset_config, update_config update_config(cache_mode="filesystem", cache_duration=3600) # keep frames on disk for an hour print(get_config()) clear_cache() # wipes the memory and filesystem entries update_config(cache_mode="off") # every call fetches reset_config() # back to the environment / defaults An unknown mode raises ValueError. The cache key is the loader's name and arguments, excluding return_as_pandas (one stored polars frame serves both), and it does not include the URL: after a release file is republished, call clear_cache(). The starting values come from environment variables, which an explicit update_config() overrides: The package-wide HTTP response cache is separate. It caches raw responses from the live wrappers by URL and parameters, with a lifetime chosen per endpoint (30 days for a finished game's play-by-play, 5 minutes for news and injuries, never for a live scoreboard or an in-progress game), and it is off by default. Control it from Python or with sdv cache on the command line: import sportsdataverse as sdv sdv.set_cache_mode("memory") # "off" (default), "memory" or "filesystem" print(sdv.cache_stats()) sdv.set_cache_mode("off")

CFBPlayProcess can rebuild a game's processed plays from a saved ESPN summary without touching the network. That is how a raw library is reprocessed after a parser fix. Two things would otherwise make requests: joining the per-play participants, and looking up the betting line when the summary's pickcenter has fewer than two providers (it is empty for 2024 and later games). The spread and total are EPA and WP inputs, so persist them with the raw JSON and pass them back as odds_override, a dict with gameSpread, overUnder, homeFavorite, gameSpreadAvailable and, optionally, overUnderAvailable. First capture the summary once: import json import tempfile from pathlib import Path raw_dir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) summary = CFBPlayProcess(gameId=401628334, raw=True).espn_cfb_pbp() (raw_dir / "401628334.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary), encoding="utf-8") odds = {"gameSpread": -4.0, "overUnder": 58.5, "homeFavorite": True, "gameSpreadAvailable": True, "overUnderAvailable": True} Then rebuild from the dict with espn_cfb_pbp(summary=...), which skips the participant requests and reads the odds from the summary or the override: offline = CFBPlayProcess(gameId=401628334, odds_override=odds) offline.espn_cfb_pbp(summary=summary) offline.run_processing_pipeline() print(offline.odds_source, offline.plays_frame.height) # injected 169 Or from the file on disk with cfb_pbp_disk(). Here join_participants=False is required, because reading from disk alone does not switch off the participant requests: from_disk = CFBPlayProcess(gameId=401628334, path_to_json=str(raw_dir), join_participants=False, odds_override=odds) from_disk.cfb_pbp_disk() from_disk.run_processing_pipeline() odds_source records where the line came from: "summary_pickcenter", "core_odds_api", "default" or "injected". A malformed odds_override raises ValueError in the constructor. Leave overUnderAvailable out only when you do not know whether the total is a market one; it is then null, never guessed.

The package reaches data two ways. Release loaders (load_<lg>_*) read parquet files that SportsDataverse producers publish to GitHub releases. A whole season comes back in one fast request, already processed (EPA, WP, cleaned names), and the same call returns the same frame tomorrow. They lag the live game by the producer's schedule, usually a day, and some keep the dtypes their files were published with. Live wrappers (espn_<lg>_*, nhl_web_*, pwhl_*, the provider families) call the source's API when you call them. They are current to the minute and reach endpoints no release covers, but you make one request per game or page, and the answer can change. from sportsdataverse.cfb import espn_cfb_schedule, load_cfb_schedule season = load_cfb_schedule([2024]) # every 2024 game, one request week_one = espn_cfb_schedule(dates=2024, week=1) # ESPN's live schedule for one week print(season.height, week_one.height) A season below a loader's floor raises SeasonNotFoundError before any request. A season the release has no file for is skipped by most loaders and raises NoDataError in a few (the NFL loaders among them); a download that failed always raises AssetFetchError, never an empty frame. See Troubleshooting.
The failures people hit most often, what each one means, and what to do about it.

Every error the package raises subclasses sportsdataverse.errors.SportsDataverseError, so one except clause catches any of them. The useful distinction is between the subclasses. NoDataError and AssetFetchError are kept apart on purpose: a rate-limited season recorded as an empty one is silent data loss. Neither subclasses the other. NoESPNDataError is the old name of NoDataError and is the same class, so existing except NoESPNDataError code keeps working. from sportsdataverse.cfb import espn_cfb_game_rosters, load_cfb_schedule from sportsdataverse.errors import AssetFetchError, NoDataError try: rosters = espn_cfb_game_rosters(game_id=1) # not a real ESPN game id except NoDataError: rosters = None # nothing there: skip it try: schedule = load_cfb_schedule([2024]) except AssetFetchError as exc: raise RuntimeError(f"fetch failed, retry later: {exc}") from exc A season below a loader's floor fails fast, before any request: from sportsdataverse.errors import SeasonNotFoundError from sportsdataverse.nba import load_nba_rosters try: load_nba_rosters([2024]) except SeasonNotFoundError as exc: print(exc) # season cannot be less than 2025

The NBA and WNBA possession and season-compile paths can read stats.nba.com payloads through a raw JSON store (SDV_PY_NBA_RAW_JSON_DIR, or raw_store_dir=). Read-only mode (SDV_PY_NBA_RAW_JSON_READONLY=1, or raw_store_readonly=True) means offline: a capture in the store is served, and a miss raises RawStoreMissError naming the endpoint and game instead of quietly going to the network. Per-game compile loops catch it, log the game and move on. # Not run here: the store falls through to stats.nba.com when writable. from sportsdataverse.errors import RawStoreMissError from sportsdataverse.nba.nba_possessions import nba_possessions try: poss = nba_possessions("0022300001", raw_store_readonly=True) except RawStoreMissError as exc: print(f"not in the raw store: {exc}")

documents.t: Parsers never raise on a payload of the wrong shape; they return a zero-row frame. To keep that frame from reading as "no data", they warn SchemaDriftWarning, naming the parser, the payload path and the exception. An id column the Int64 cast refuses also warns it. In a pipeline that must never publish a drifted parse, turn it into an error: import warnings from sportsdataverse.errors import SchemaDriftWarning warnings.filterwarnings("error", category=SchemaDriftWarning) The other package warnings, all UserWarning subclasses in sportsdataverse.errors: EmptyResponseWarning: a stats.nba.com / stats.wnba.com call came back 2xx with an empty object. The usual cause is a missing or invalid parameter, most often Season. EraCoverageWarning: NFL model features were built for a season past the last validated era. AsOfCutWarning: a pregame projection could not place its target game in time. UnsupportedPageFormatWarning: a scraped page is in a layout its parser does not read.

stats.nba.com and stats.wnba.com fingerprint the TLS handshake and also judge the IP address. From a datacenter or cloud address (CI runners, Colab, most cloud VMs) a request does not fail: it stalls until it times out. Run these wrappers from a residential connection. The per-request timeout is SDV_PY_NBA_STATS_TIMEOUT (seconds, default 30); raise it for slow historical endpoints. Retries are set with SDV_PY_NBA_STATS_RETRIES. # Not run here: stats.nba.com stalls on cloud IPs. from sportsdataverse.nba import nba_stats df = nba_stats.nba_stats_leaguedashplayerstats(league_id="00") # NBA gleague = nba_stats.nba_stats_leaguedashplayerstats(league_id="20") # G League

Plain requests is fingerprint-blocked by stats.nba.com, so the runtime uses curl_cffi with Chrome impersonation. It is an optional dependency (in the tests and all extras), imported only when a live call is made: pip install curl_cffi # or pip install "sportsdataverse[all]" A few international basketball sites (live FIBA game pages, P. LEAGUE+) need it too.

The test suite gates live tests with SDV_PY_LIVE_TESTS=1. The stats.nba.com / stats.wnba.com tests use a separate gate, SDV_PY_NBA_STATS_LIVE=1, which no CI workflow sets, because those hosts hang on CI runners. To run them, from a residential IP: SDV_PY_NBA_STATS_LIVE=1 uv run pytest tests/nba -k nba_stats
documents.s: Why do the stats.nba.com tests skip?

documents.t: stats.ncaa.org bans IP addresses quickly, so the package never fetches it directly. Every request goes through the shared NCAA fetch layer (mbb_ncaa_fetch / wbb_ncaa_fetch), which: requires a proxy: without one it raises RuntimeError (a setup error, not a fetch failure); caches every page it fetches under ~/.sportsdataverse/ncaa_cache and serves the cache first, so a page is fetched once; raises NoDataError on a real 404 and AssetFetchError for a banned or exhausted proxy pool, an uncleared bm-verify challenge or the Terms gate. Configure it with environment variables (SDV_PY_NCAA_PROXY_URL, SDV_PY_NCAA_CACHE_DIR, SDV_PY_NCAA_TIMEOUT, SDV_PY_NCAA_ROTATE_EVERY, ...) or programmatically. Never write your own requests against stats.ncaa.org; reuse this layer. # Not run here: stats.ncaa.org bans cloud IPs. from sportsdataverse.mbb import ncaa_mbb_play_by_play from sportsdataverse.mbb.mbb_ncaa_fetch import update_config update_config(proxy_url="http://user:password@203.0.113.10:8080") pbp = ncaa_mbb_play_by_play([5254137, 5254138], errors="skip") # scrape_status says why a game dropped With the default errors="raise", a failed game raises AssetFetchError rather than being dropped, so a ban never reads as a smaller season.

The NFL loaders (load_nfl_*) cache their frames: in memory by default, or on disk with cache_mode="filesystem", for cache_duration seconds (24 hours by default). The cache key is the loader's name and arguments. It does not include the URL, so if a release file is republished under the same name, or the package changes the path a loader reads, you keep getting the cached frame until it expires. Clear it, or turn caching off while you debug: from sportsdataverse.nfl import clear_cache, update_config clear_cache() # drops the memory and filesystem entries update_config(cache_mode="off") # no caching for the rest of the session The SDV_PY_NFL_CACHE environment variable sets the starting mode. The package-wide HTTP response cache (sdv cache ..., sportsdataverse.cache) is a different cache, off by default; see the cache recipe.

If your test suite turns warnings into errors (pytest's -W error or filterwarnings = error), these are the package warnings you are likely to meet: DeprecationWarning from a moved or deprecated import path: sportsdataverse.parsed.* (call sportsdataverse.<league> directly) or a league that moved, such as sportsdataverse.epl (now sportsdataverse.soccer.epl). Fix the import; the message names the new path. SchemaDriftWarning, EmptyResponseWarning and the others above. Each says something real about the data, so assert it (pytest.warns(SchemaDriftWarning)) where you expect it, or filter that one message where it is incidental. Avoid ignoring a whole category. import sportsdataverse itself emits no warnings.

sportsdataverse.basketball.ibba — 16 endpoints. Note: Access: unofficial and reverse-engineered, keyless, for internal use. The wrappers read basket.co.il's ASP.NET web service (the ops its own site calls) and space requests at least one second apart; keep crawls slow and incremental. Payloads are not redistributed as release assets. Contact details (e-mail, phone, fax) and coaches' dates of birth are dropped by the parsers. Note: Season and ids. season is the END year and the host's own cYear (2026 = 2025-26): no mapping. team_id and player_id are per-SEASON registrations (Maccabi Tel Aviv = team 1109 in 2025-26, 2111 in 2026-27; the ASMX host has no cross-season person id: the stable key is the Segev player id in ibba_segev_*). team_uid is the stable club id (Maccabi = 10). ibba_games.segev_game_id joins ibba_segev_* game_id from 2025-26. Note: Coverage: league box scores from 2004-05 (season=2005); external_id / segev_game_id only from 2025-26; the women's league and Liga Leumit are NOT on this host (they are on Genius Sports org IBBA and in Segev). Every ASMX value is a string and Hebrew text is HTML-entity encoded; the parsers cast ids, counts and dates and unescape text. An unknown id answers an empty body (NoDataError); box scores of unfinished games are refused.

sportsdataverse.basketball.ibba — 6 endpoints. Note: Access: Segev Stats is the live-stats vendor behind basket.co.il's game pages; its JSON-RPC API is keyless, unofficial and not documented for outside use. The wrappers space requests at least one second apart and read only finished games; payloads are not redistributed as release assets. The host serves JSON as text/html. Note: Games and ids. game_id is one flat Segev id space across seasons AND competitions: men's Winner League, Winner Cup, women's, Leumit, youth, school and pre-season games share it, so read competition from ibba_segev_game_info (team names do not separate men from women reliably). There is no game list: league game ids come from ibba_games.segev_game_id (2025-26 on), the women's league and Leumit from a scan or Genius Sports org IBBA. Segev team and player ids are stable across seasons (Jaylen Hoard = player 1000 in games 50 and 419), unlike the IBBA season registrations, and are not IBBA ids. Note: Play-by-play: actions name the player by Segev id and by JERSEY number, score reads away-home, and shot x / y are one half-court frame (x 0-1470 across, basket near 735; y out from the baseline, rim near 112-140); which sideline is x = 0 and the metric scale are unverified. Segev renamed its team game stats between 2025-26 and 2026-27; the parsers unify them. Unfinished games and ids of another game are refused.

sportsdataverse-py gives the community free, tidy, analysis-ready sports data in Python. It is the Python member of the SportsDataverse family and deliberately mirrors its R sisters — hoopR (NBA/MBB), wehoop (WNBA/WBB), cfbfastR (CFB), baseballr (MLB), and fastRhockey (NHL/PWHL) — so the function you know in R is the function you call in Python. The NFL module mirrors the nflverse's nflreadpy, and the package plays well with the wider PySport ecosystem. Beyond aggregation and tidying, the project also exists to make open-source expected-points and win-probability models reproducible and benchmarkable, especially for American football. New here? Read Ecosystem & philosophy for the design philosophy, the full function-naming paradigm, and how the Python and R packages line up.

pip install --pre sportsdataverse --pre installs the 0.2.0 beta, which these docs describe. Without it pip picks the last stable release, 0.1.4. # Today's NBA scoreboard: a polars DataFrame by default from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_scoreboard df = espn_nba_scoreboard() # → polars print(df.select(["game_id", "home_name", "away_name", "home_score", "away_score"]).head()) raw = espn_nba_scoreboard(return_parsed=False) # → the raw Dict # Aaron Judge's 2024 season stats from the official MLB API from sportsdataverse.mlb import mlb_person_stats, parse_mlb_api_person_stats judge = parse_mlb_api_person_stats( mlb_person_stats(person_id=592450, stats="season", season=2024) ) print(judge.select(["stats_group", "stat_home_runs", "stat_avg"])) # Connor McDavid's 2024-25 EDGE skating speed profile from sportsdataverse.nhl import nhl_edge_skater_detail, parse_edge_detail mcdavid = parse_edge_detail(nhl_edge_skater_detail(8478402)) print(mcdavid.select(["player_first_name_default", "top_shot_speed_metric"])) Parser-backed wrappers return a polars DataFrame by default; see Polars / pandas parser layer below.

NoDataError — the fetch SUCCEEDED and there is nothing there (a 404, or ESPN's 200-with-code:404 body). AssetFetchError — the fetch FAILED and the answer is unknown (403, rate limit, exhausted retries). Never record this as an empty season. ValueError — a 400 / 422: the request itself is wrong, so retrying cannot help. The hand-written ESPN scrapers and every generated flat-API getter raise rather than returning an error body or an empty dict.

sdv-docs is an MCP server over a prebuilt index of this surface — exact columns, function signatures, provider endpoints and released datasets: claude mcp add sdv-docs -- uvx --from 'sportsdataverse[mcp]>=0.2.0b1' sdv-docs It needs the mcp extra, sportsdataverse 0.2.0b1 or newer and Python >= 3.10. Without the >=0.2.0b1 pin, uv resolves 0.1.4, which has no sdv-docs.

The parser layer in sportsdataverse._common_espn_parsers (plus matching modules for the MLB and NHL sibling APIs) turns raw payloads into tidy polars (or pandas) DataFrames. ESPN wrappers with a parser default to return_parsed=True. Pass return_parsed=False to recover the raw Dict, or return_as_pandas=True to get a pandas DataFrame: from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_team_roster df = espn_nba_team_roster(team_id=13) # → polars (default) raw = espn_nba_team_roster(team_id=13, return_parsed=False) # → Dict pdf = espn_nba_team_roster(team_id=13, return_as_pandas=True) # → pandas For NHL / MLB sibling-API wrappers, compose the wrapper with its parser: from sportsdataverse.nhl import nhl_web_pbp, parse_nhl_web_pbp df = parse_nhl_web_pbp(nhl_web_pbp(2023030417)) # 331-row polars frame See the Architecture and Parsers pages for full details. Deprecated sportsdataverse.parsed.* is deprecated. The league wrappers already default to return_parsed=True, so call sportsdataverse.nba (etc.) directly; the parsed namespace is a thin alias kept for back-compat. See Migrating to 0.2.0.

pip install --pre sportsdataverse (or uv add --prerelease allow sportsdataverse) while 0.2.0 is in beta. The Install & CLI guide covers uv, the optional extras, the supported Python and polars versions, the sdv command line and the sdv-docs MCP server.

To cite the sportsdataverse-py Python package in publications, use: BibTeX Citation @misc{gilani_sdvpy_2021, author = {Gilani, Saiem}, title = {sportsdataverse-py: The SportsDataverse's Python Package for Sports Data.}, url = {https://py.sportsdataverse.org}, year = {2021} }

sportsdataverse.basketball.kbl — 22 endpoints. Note: Unofficial and unsupported: these wrappers read api.kbl.or.kr, the data API behind the www.kbl.or.kr React site (stats vendor sports2i). No key, cookie or proxy is needed, but two request headers must be present (Channel and TeamCode; the runtime sends WEB and XX). www.kbl.or.kr/robots.txt returns the SPA's HTML and api.kbl.or.kr/robots.txt a 500 error envelope, so no policy or Crawl-delay is published (checked 2026-10-12); the site's terms (/terms/list) were not reviewed for data reuse. The runtime waits at least 1 s before every request, retries included. Payloads are not redistributed as release assets. Note: Not wrapped: the site's /record/* and /player/player/{pcode} pages are rendered by the sports2i widget from two other hosts (kbl-api.sports2i.com and api-stats.kbl.or.kr: team four factors, clutch, hustle, shot dashboards, all-time leaders) and need their own intake. WKBL (the women's league) is out of scope by owner ruling. Note: Seasons are END years (2026 = 2025-26). KBL numbers seasons AND D-League (reserve league) editions with one sequential seasonCode; division picks 'kbl' or 'd_league' and game_code the competition inside the season, and kbl_runtime sends the API's glkey. The playoff routes take the REGULAR-SEASON key; the old route serves seasonCode below 45 and the new one 45 on, and the wrapper picks it. Note: Ids: gmkey S{seasonCode}G{gameCode}N{gameNo} (a string, an object only inside the new playoff bracket), team_code (two-digit string with a leading zero, not stable across ownership changes) and pcode (six-digit string, the same on every route). The play-by-play carries no pcode: join its player_name to the game's box score on name and team_code. isEnded is unreliable (0 on every finished game through 2005-06), so a game is final when isEnded is 1 or when it is dated before today (KST), both teams scored and its play-by-play reached the game-end row; anything else raises AssetFetchError. The first game call also fetches the header (and, for such a game, the play-by-play) once; the answer is cached for the process. Note: Coverage: box scores and play-by-play from the first season (1997); shot x/y from 2006-07 (an earlier game's shot chart is empty: a zero-row frame); advanced rates are filled from 1997-98 on (the vendor computes them from the box); screen assists and deflections are 0 before the recent seasons. fg is TWO-point field goals made (dunks included), fgt all field goals, and a made dunk is its own row in the play-by-play. Shot x/y are pixels on the site's 726 x 412 full-court image; basket names the target end and teams switch at half-time, so normalise with basket before stacking shots.

khl_club_crosswalk(season: 'Optional[int]' = None, stage: 'Optional[str]' = 'regular', *, tournament_id: 'Optional[int]' = None, return_as_pandas: 'bool' = False, **kwargs: 'Any') -> 'Frame' Club id <-> team-season id for one tournament, read from a covering set of game headers. Fetches the schedule, picks the fewest games (greedy) that touch every club, fetches those game headers (about 15 requests, each waiting its polite second) and maps the ids they carry. Parameters Returns polars.DataFrame | pandas.DataFrame: tournament_id, club_id (stable), team_season_id (this tournament's), one row per club. Raises Example from sportsdataverse.hockey.khl import khl_club_crosswalk xw = khl_club_crosswalk(season=2026) xw.filter(xw["club_id"] == 7)

khl_club_crosswalk_from_frames(*frames: 'Any', return_as_pandas: 'bool' = False) -> 'Frame' Club id <-> team-season id from frames that carry both (game header / info, player career). Parameters Returns polars.DataFrame | pandas.DataFrame: one row per (tournament_id, club_id, team_season_id), all Int64, sorted; zero rows when no frame carries a pair. Raises Example from sportsdataverse.hockey.khl import khl_club_crosswalk_from_frames, khl_game_header khl_club_crosswalk_from_frames(khl_game_header(898236, season=2026))

sportsdataverse.basketball.kzs — 23 endpoints. Note: Unofficial and unsupported: these wrappers read the public read API (Java/Spring, built by OnixWeb) that the kzs.si site itself calls. No terms of use were located (unverified), api.kzs.si/robots.txt answers 401 and www.kzs.si/robots.txt 404, so no policy or Crawl-delay is published. The runtime waits at least 1 s before every request, retries included. Payloads are not redistributed as release assets. Note: Personal data: the API serves officials' and coaches' emails, phones and home towns, and clubs' bank accounts and addresses, publicly. The parsers never output them (officials appear by name only; club addresses, personnel and the commissioner report are dropped). Do not add them back. Note: Seasons are END years (2027 = 2026/2027); KZS' own season ids are opaque (27 = 2026/2027) and the runtime maps them. Competition ids are per season. Three team keys are never interchangeable: the match-team id (per match and side), team_id (one club team in one season) and club_id (across seasons). player_id is the registry id, person_id the person behind it. Note: Errors are HTTP 400 for everything (an unknown id and a bad parameter alike), so the runtime raises ValueError for it, never an empty frame. List routes default to 150 rows with no truncation signal: every list wrapper asks for a large limit and refuses a full page. The play-by-play and box-score wrappers, the leaderboards, teams, rounds and playing days each make one extra, cached request (the match header or the competition) to prove the answer is the one asked for and the game is final. Note: Coverage: scores from 2007/08; box scores and play-by-play from 2015/16. Some 2020/21 men's games have a box score but no play-by-play (NoDataError): the Genius data.json (genius_match_id in kzs_matches) is the fallback. Shot x/y are Genius court percent; side (LEFT/RIGHT) names the basket end and teams switch ends at half time, so normalise with side before stacking shots. Advanced box-score fields are 0 in every observed game.
